title: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: undecidability can have quite obvious effects even with a very simple underlying rule and very simple initial conditions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Undecidability and Intractability” (from p. 753), p. 755. Scope: 4-color totalistic cellular automaton with code 1004600 and simple programs generally

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-20: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The finite numerical observations are directly reproducible with modest public computation. The stronger interpretation that these trajectories demonstrate undecidability is not established by finite runs, but the stated concrete behavior can be checked now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reimplement totalistic rule 1004600, enumerate the specified simple initial conditions, and record extinction time and population through ten million steps. Reproducing both a greater-than-1000-step extinction and continuing growth at ten million confirms the concrete observation; failure under the documented convention refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite non-extinction does not itself establish undecidability.

The exact initial-condition convention must be reconstructed.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The reported life histories are a finite computation that current simulators can repeat, so the step counts and widths can be confirmed or refuted now. The framing that these histories are effects of undecidability is a further claim. A long unresolved run is what an undecidable question would look like in practice, and it is also what a very long transient looks like.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Simulate the 4-color totalistic rule with code 1004600 from the simple seeds in the figure and compare death times and widths with the reported figures, including death after 1017 steps and continued growth past ten million steps. Those counts are checkable; treating the unfinished runs as undecidability requires a proof that no algorithm decides eventual death.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A long finite transient has the same appearance as an undecidable infinite-time question.

A pattern still growing after ten million steps may later die or become periodic.
